text:
Here are two hundred thousand customers, each with a satisfaction score out of a hundred. Their true average is seventy. But say you can only ask five hundred of them. Does it matter WHICH five hundred? Pick them at random, and their average comes out at sixty-nine point six. A little low... but close. Now take the five hundred who are easiest to reach. Happy customers answer surveys, so say anyone above seventy-five is eleven times as likely to be picked. This sample averages eighty and a half. That's more than ten points too high.

Was that just bad luck? Draw again... and again, a hundred times each. The random averages land on both sides of seventy, about half above and half below. The easy ones land near eighty, every single time. A miss that always points the same way has a name. It's bias.

So here's the obvious fix. Ask more people. Grow both samples from fifty customers to twenty thousand. Both get steadier as they grow, and at about the same pace. But only the random one is closing in on seventy. The easy sample just becomes a sharper and sharper estimate of the WRONG number. At twenty thousand, one customer in ten, it's rock steady... and still almost ten points high.

This went wrong for real in nineteen thirty-six. The Literary Digest mailed out ten million ballots for the presidential race. Nearly two point four million came back. A huge sample... but the people who chose to reply leaned toward the challenger, Alf Landon. So the Digest called it for Landon, with Roosevelt on just forty-three percent. George Gallup asked far fewer people, chosen to mirror the voters, and put Roosevelt on fifty-six. Roosevelt got sixty-two and a half, and won every state but two. Two point four million answers couldn't fix who was answering.

So every estimate can miss in two ways. Variance is the scatter from one sample to the next. More data shrinks it. Bias is where the scatter is centered, and more data leaves it right where it was. Only a better method moves the center.
